summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for acute exacerbation of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, presenting with worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral leg edema. The exacerbation was attributed to medication nonadherence, particularly with torsemide, ramipril, and metoprolol. Initial labs showed elevated BNP and pseudohyperkalemia, with true hypokalemia requiring repletion. Treatment included IV diuresis with transition to oral torsemide 80 mg daily, increased ramipril to twice daily, spironolactone uptitrated to 50 mg, and continuation of warfarin at 2.5 mg daily after a transient hold. Echocardiogram revealed reduced LVEF of 30% with global hypokinesis. Serial chest X-rays demonstrated significant improvement in pulmonary edema. The patient stabilized, was discharged home on optimized heart failure regimen, with instructions to monitor weight, follow up on labs, and consider restarting allopurinol for gout prevention.
problems: Acute on chronic combined systolic (congestive) and diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with unspecified diabetic retinopathy without macular edema
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
